title: tenho feito
summary: I've been doing (lately): a trap for English speakers
intro: Tenho + past participle looks like English "I have done", but it means something different: an action repeated or ongoing up to now. Tenho trabalhado muito = I've been working a lot (lately).
For one finished event, even where English says "have", Portuguese uses the simple past: Já viste o filme? = Have you seen the film?
Only ter changes (tenho, tens, tem, temos, têm). The participle stays the same: -ar verbs end in -ado, -er and -ir verbs in -ido. Some are irregular:

examples.en: Lately I've been working a lot.
Have you seen the film? (one event: simple past)

notes: Como tens passado? (How have you been?) is a friendly question to someone you haven't seen for a while.
Words that go with it: ultimamente (lately), nos últimos tempos, esta semana, este mês.

drills.en: Lately I've been working a lot.
It's been very hot this week.
How have you been?
She hasn't been sleeping well.
They've been watching a lot of Portuguese films.
We haven't been going out much this month.
I've been writing a lot of emails.
How have you been?
I haven't been sleeping well.
Have you seen the film?
drills.why: One finished event: the simple past. Tens visto would mean "have you been seeing".

drills.en: I've been working a lot lately.
drills.why: Ongoing up to now (ultimamente): tenho + participle.

drills.en: She went to Lisbon yesterday.
drills.why: Ontem, one finished event: the simple past.

title: tinha feito
intro: Tinha + past participle = had done, something that happened before another moment in the past: Quando cheguei, o comboio já tinha partido = When I arrived, the train had already left.
Only ter changes (tinha, tinhas, tinha, tínhamos, tinham). The participles are the ones from the previous topic.

examples.pt: Quando cheguei, o comboio já tinha partido.
examples.en: When I arrived, the train had already left.
I had never seen the sea.

examples.pt: Ela disse que já tinha comido.
examples.en: She said she had already eaten.
We had arranged to meet at eight.

notes: Já (already) and nunca (never) often go with it.
In books you'll also meet an older one-word form: falara, fizera (= tinha falado, tinha feito). Recognise it; you don't need to use it.

drills.en: When I arrived, the train had already left.
I had never seen the sea.
She said she had already eaten.
We had already made dinner when they arrived.
Had you been to Portugal before?
They had said they were coming.
I had never seen the sea.
She had already left.
When I arrived, they had already had dinner.

drills.before: Quando cheguei à estação, o comboio já
drills.en: When I got to the station, the train had already left.
drills.why: It happened before another past moment (when I arrived): tinha + participle.

drills.after: o mar pela primeira vez em 2019.
drills.en: I saw the sea for the first time in 2019.
drills.why: One event at a clear time: the simple past.

drills.en: She said she had read the book.
drills.why: Something earlier than a past moment (she said): tinha + participle.
